items.readable_text:
Content:
The column space of a matrix [MATH: A] is denoted [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] and is the span of the columns of [MATH: A] (i.e., the set of all possible linear combinations of columns of [MATH: A]). For example, consider the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [1|3; 2|− 1]]
where we denote its columns by [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},] respectively. The column space of this matrix is given by
[MATH: [1; 2]]

Content:
Now, suppose we would like to determine whether the vector [MATH: [2; − 3]] lies in [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A).] In other words, we need to check if [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.] So, we need to determine whether [MATH: \mathbf{b}] can be written as some linear combination of [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: x_{1}a_{1} + x_{2}a_{2} = b]

Content:
Notice that the equation above can be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [a_{1}|a_{2}][x_{1}; x_{2}]|= b; [1|3; 2|− 1]_(⏟)_(A)[x_{1}; x_{2}]_(⏟)_(x)|= [2; − 3]_(⏟)_(b)]

Content:
So, the equation is equivalent to [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.] To solve the equation, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix [MATH: [A \,|\, \mathbf{b}]] as follows:
[MATH: [A|b]|= [1|3|2; 2|− 1|− 3]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 2)R_{1}; ∼[1|3|2; 0|− 7|− 7]]

Content:
Now, we have the system
[MATH: {x_{1} + 3x_{2} = 2; − 7x_{2} = − 7.]

Content:
From the second equation, we get [MATH: x_2=1.] Substituting into the first equation, we get [MATH: x_1=-1.]

Content:
Since we have a solution, the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] is consistent, which implies that [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Col}(A).]

Content:
Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write [MATH: \mathbf{b}] as a linear combination of [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [2; − 3]]

sections.normalized_html: The column space is defined for matrices of any dimensions. In general, if [MATH: {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n}] are the columns of a matrix [MATH: A,] that is to say, [MATH: |||||; a_{1}|a_{2}|…|a_{n};|||||] then [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A) = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n} \}.]

sections.readable_text: The column space satisfies the following properties:

sections.normalized_html:
• If [MATH: A] is an [MATH: {\color{blue}m}\times n] matrix, then [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A)] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^{\color{blue}m}.] This is because each column has [MATH: {\color{blue}m}] entries.

  • [MATH: \mathbf{b}\in\textrm{Col}(A)] if and only if the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] is consistent (has a solution).

  • If the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] is inconsistent (has no solution), then [MATH: \mathbf{b}\not\in\textrm{Col}(A).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The column space of a matrix [MATH: A] is denoted [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] and is the span of the columns of [MATH: A] (i.e., the set of all possible linear combinations of columns of [MATH: A]). For example, consider the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [1|3; 2|− 1]]
where we denote its columns by [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},] respectively. The column space of this matrix is given by
[MATH: [1; 2]]

Content:
Now, suppose we would like to determine whether the vector [MATH: [2; − 3]] lies in [MATH: \textrm{Col}(A).] In other words, we need to check if [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.] So, we need to determine whether [MATH: \mathbf{b}] can be written as some linear combination of [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: x_{1}a_{1} + x_{2}a_{2} = b]

Content:
Notice that the equation above can be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [a_{1}|a_{2}][x_{1}; x_{2}]|= b; [1|3; 2|− 1]_(⏟)_(A)[x_{1}; x_{2}]_(⏟)_(x)|= [2; − 3]_(⏟)_(b)]

Content:
So, the equation is equivalent to [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.] To solve the equation, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix [MATH: [A \,|\, \mathbf{b}]] as follows:
[MATH: [A|b]|= [1|3|2; 2|− 1|− 3]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (− 2)R_{1}; ∼[1|3|2; 0|− 7|− 7]]

Content:
Now, we have the system
[MATH: {x_{1} + 3x_{2} = 2; − 7x_{2} = − 7.]

Content:
From the second equation, we get [MATH: x_2=1.] Substituting into the first equation, we get [MATH: x_1=-1.]

Content:
Since we have a solution, the equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] is consistent, which implies that [MATH: \mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Col}(A).]

Content:
Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write [MATH: \mathbf{b}] as a linear combination of [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}_1] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [2; − 3]]
